overview.title: Content compass
overview.html:
"In Vesperine, every promise is sealed with a kiss. Last night, one of those kisses killed a man."

Content compass: Mature fantasy intrigue — flirtation, seduction-as-strategy, scandal, vice, betrayal, and violence. Romance and sexual content are always suggestive, never explicit, and fade to black between consenting adults. Nothing romantic or sexual ever involves captives, coercion, or anyone underage. The ogress den is played as danger plus bawdy comedy, not titillation at a prisoner's expense. Use your table's preferred safety tools (Lines & Veils, an X-card, or a quick "too far? → cut to morning" agreement).

Recommended levels: Characters of levels 3–8. The central mystery works at any point in that range; the side adventures are tiered (see each one).

overview.title: Rules: D&D 2024 (5.5e) · SRD 5.2.1
overview.html: The world guide's header says "D&D 5e compatible" and names SRD creatures (D&D 5e compatible. Stat blocks reference creatures from the 5e SRD / Monster Manual by name (e.g., spy, veteran, ogre, vampire spawn) with suggested tweaks.). DM Atlas runs this campaign with the 2024 rules (SRD 5.2.1) only. Creature names in the text are linked to DM Atlas's SRD 5.2.1 stat blocks where the names match, using the 2024 names: thug → Tough, veteran → Warrior Veteran, kobold → Kobold Warrior. There is no SRD 5.2.1 stat block for pixie, winged kobold or giant moth; the guide's own notes for those (e.g. giant moths use Giant Bat or Giant Wasp stats) still apply. The 128 creatures in the Bestiary tab are the Carnelia Bestiary's own 2024-rules stat blocks.

overview.title: The World: Carnelia
overview.html: Carnelia is a sun-drenched, wine-dark land of canals, vineyards, and old magic, ruled less by kings than by contracts. Five hundred years ago the founders of its greatest city struck a bargain with the Fae Duke of the Dusk — the Accord of Lips — which made any promise sealed with a kiss magically binding. The Accord made Carnelia rich: merchants, nobles, and lovers alike trust a kissed contract more than any gold. It also made Carnelia dangerous. A kiss here can be a love letter, a business deal, a marriage, a confession, a curse, or a death sentence.

overview.title: The Premise
overview.html:
Every kiss-oath sworn in Carnelia is recorded, in shimmering ink that writes itself, in the Ledger of Vows — a living book kept by a single magically appointed guardian, the Oathwarden. The Ledger is the spine of society: it settles disputes, proves marriages, enforces debts, and keeps the Fae Duke's ancient bargain intact.

At midnight on the Night of Unmasking — the final night of the city's month-long masquerade festival — the Oathwarden, Lord Aurelian Sable, was found dead in the Rosewater Gallery of the Velvet Opera, his lips stained black as ink, moments after kissing the city's most famous diva in front of a hundred masked witnesses.

Now the Ledger has no keeper. Each night that passes without a new Oathwarden, oaths begin to unravel. Marriages dissolve mid-dinner. Debts vanish — or double. Old curses wake. And on the seventh night, the Accord itself will fail, and the Fae Duke will come to collect what the city owes him.

The characters are handed a Red Ribbon Warrant — the Opera Council's sealed authority to question anyone, enter anywhere, and name the killer before the seventh bell.

overview.title: Tone & Themes
overview.html:
• Seductive intrigue. Flirtation is a weapon, a currency, and a lie detector. Everyone in Vesperine is flirting with someone, usually for a reason.
  • Masks and true faces. Who you pretend to be versus who you are — and what you'd give to be seen.
  • Promises and their price. A world where words literally bind makes every bargain a moral choice.
  • Decadence with teeth. Silk sheets, poisoned wine, velvet-gloved threats. Comedy and danger share the same bed (figuratively).
  • Consent matters here — in-world, too. The Accord of Lips cannot bind an unwilling kiss; a forced or stolen kiss creates no oath. This is a known, sacred law, and violators are reviled. (It's also a plot clue.)

overview.title: The Hub City: Vesperine, the City of Masks
overview.html:
Vesperine is built on a hundred islands knit together by bridges, gondola lanes, and gossip. Lanterns of colored glass hang over every canal, so the night city glows rose, amber, violet, and green. Masks are legal — even fashionable — everywhere, at all hours, and showing your bare face in a salon is considered either very brave or very forward.

At a glance
Population ~60,000 (humans, half-elves, tieflings, elves, halflings; a famous minority of satyrs and fauns in the theater district)
Government The Opera Council — seven patrons of the Velvet Opera who own most of the city's debt. Officially "advisory." Actually everything.
Law The Lantern Watch (underpaid, overdressed)
Currency Gold ducats and silver kisses (a coin stamped with lips — a joke that became official)
Notable vices Masquerades, card salons, wine of the Vinehold, dream-moth dust, duelling for love
What visitors notice The smell of rosewater and canal water; the music never stops; everyone touches your arm when they talk

Key districts of Vesperine

  1. The Gilded Crescent — Noble palazzos facing the Grand Canal. Balconies built for eavesdropping. Home of House Morrow and the shuttered Sable Palazzo.
  2. The Velvet Quarter — Theaters, salons, pleasure-gardens, and the Velvet Opera, a cathedral of red plush and gold leaf. The Rosewater Gallery (the murder scene) is on its second tier.
  3. Needle Row — Artisans' lanes: tailors, wigmakers, perfumers, and the Atelier of Madame Rook, the city's most beloved maskmaker.
  4. The Drowned Market — A half-sunken flea market under the old city, where the Thorn Syndicate sells anything, including secrets and people's debts.
  5. The Hall of Vows — A white-marble temple-library on its own island, where the Ledger of Vows rests on a lectern of living rose-thorn. Tended by the Veiled Sisters.
  6. Lanternside — Docks, taverns, sailors, and the Lantern Watch's leaning headquarters, "the Tilted House."

sessions.title: Prologue — Through the Oathless Glass
sessions.summary: Optional opening: the party is pulled out of its own world through the Oathless Glass.

scenes.title: Introduction
scenes.html:
"Everyone has kissed a mirror once. A wish, a dare, a promise whispered to your own face at three in the morning. You thought no one was listening. Something was."

This optional prologue pulls the player characters out of their own world (a modern Earth, another campaign setting, anywhere) and into Carnelia. It works with brand-new characters or with an existing party crossing over from another campaign. If you'd rather start natives of Carnelia in Vesperine, skip this part; the rest of the guide works without it.

scenes.title: The Lore of the Glass
scenes.html:
Who made it. Five hundred years ago, when the founders of Vesperine struck the Accord of Lips with the Fae Duke of the Dusk, Lady Oriane Sable, the first of House Sable, did not trust the bargain. She asked for one more clause: the Oathless Clause. If the Ledger of Vows ever lost its keeper, the next Oathwarden would have to be judged (witnessed and confirmed) by someone bound by no oath in Carnelia, so that no one could rig the succession with debts and promises.

The Duke laughed and agreed. Everyone in Carnelia swears kiss-oaths from childhood on (I promise, cross my heart, kiss my thumb), so nobody born there could ever be truly oathless. Oriane answered by commissioning the Duke's own glass-wright, a fey artisan called Mirelle of the Thousand Faces, to build a mirror that could reach into other worlds and bring the oathless home. Its silver was quenched in Ledger ink. Its frame was carved from the same living rose-thorn as the Ledger's lectern. It is called the Oathless Glass.

Where it is. The Glass is the great central pane of the mirror wall in the Rosewater Gallery of the Velvet Opera, right beside the secret door to the Dressing Gallery. Hardly anyone in Vesperine remembers it is anything more than a very old, very flattering mirror. During the Duke's first collection, centuries ago, the Glass cracked, and shards of it scattered across many worlds. They turn up as antique hand-mirrors, bar-room mirrors, a dark phone screen, a still pond, a polished spoon.

Why it pulls people. A kiss on glass is a promise to the Glass: a kiss blown at your reflection, a whispered vow to your own face ("I'll be braver tomorrow," "I'll find someone who sees me," "I'll never go back to him"). The Ledger records every such reflected promise from every world in its back pages, a section the Veiled Sisters call the Margins. When an Oathwarden dies, the Glass wakes and calls the people in the Margins whose promises are still unkept. They are oathless in Carnelia, and they have unfinished business with themselves. It pulls them through to judge the next Oathwarden and to keep their promise.

Why it woke now. At midnight on the Night of Unmasking, Aurelian Sable died a few feet in front of the Glass. For the first time in thirty years, the Oathless Clause is active.

Who was summoned last time. Thirty years ago, when the previous Oathwarden died, the Glass called a single outsider, a singer named Sabine Velour (see Gateway Characters). She "judged" the succession and endorsed young Aurelian Sable with a kiss. She has regretted it ever since.

Tie to Dame Ottoline. When Ottoline tells the PCs they "have no oaths in this city," she means it literally. The Opera Council knows what the Glass does, and the Council's charter says an oathless judge must confirm the next Oathwarden. That is why the PCs get the Red Ribbon Warrant: the city cannot crown anyone without them.

scenes.title: Rules for Travelers Through the Glass
scenes.html:
• Glass-Marked. A traveler's reflection lags half a heartbeat behind them. Fey, the Veiled Sisters, and anyone who studies a mirror carefully (Perception DC 15) can tell. A traveler's reflection always shows their true face, even under a mask or a disguise spell, and so does everyone else's: the fey's human guises included (see Part 6, Glamours & Reveals). It's a handicap for infiltration and a useful tool for unmasking others ("Stand next to me in front of that mirror, Madame Rook").
  • Oathless. Travelers are immune to the Unravelling: their own words don't decay, and old Carnelian curses don't recognize them. A kiss-oath they choose to swear is twice as strong (the GM may grant advantage on any check to enforce or invoke it).
  • Anchors. Every kiss-oath a traveler swears in Carnelia, whether a bargain, a romantic vow, or a dare sealed on the lips, becomes an Anchor. Anchors are freely chosen, and the Accord rejects any kiss that is forced, tricked out of someone who didn't understand it, or given under mind-affecting magic. An Anchor binds the traveler to Carnelia until the oath is kept or the other party freely releases it. Track Anchors on the character sheet.
  • Reflection Drift (optional). At each dawn in Carnelia, each traveler rolls a d6. On a 1, their reflection does something on its own (roll on the table below). If a traveler is still in Carnelia when the seventh bell tolls without having kept their mirror-promise, their reflection stays behind for good: part of them belongs to Carnelia forever. (A hearty, bittersweet hook rather than a punishment.)
d6 Reflection Drift
1 Your reflection winks at someone you were talking to. They wink back.
2 Your reflection mouths a word: the answer to a riddle you haven't solved yet (GM's choice whether it's right).
3 Your reflection is wearing something far more daring than you are, and passers-by comment on it.
4 Your reflection points toward a clue in the room.
5 Your reflection is crying. It won't say why until you keep your promise.
6 Your reflection is missing for an hour. Somewhere in the city, people swear they saw you.

Session-zero prompt: Each player writes down the promise their character once made to their own reflection. That unkept promise is why the Glass chose them, and keeping it is part of the way home.

scenes.title: Gateway Characters
scenes.html:
Five enchanting figures each found a way to reach through the Glass or one of its shards, and each wants the PCs for reasons of their own. Every one of them is an adult, every one flirts with intent, and none of them can force a kiss-oath. They must persuade, which makes them excellent schemers. Each also has an Allure track (see Part 8), and romance with a willing PC is possible and fades to black.

The five gateway characters (Lysander, Sabine Velour, Prince Caelum, Marisol Tidewhisper and Sir Valentin Dusk) are in the NPCs tab, each with a portrait, flirt angle and secret agenda.

scenes.title: Read-Aloud: Pulled Through the Glass
scenes.html:
(Read the first paragraph, then insert the gateway character's arrival from their entry below, then finish with the last paragraph.)

It's late. The room is quiet except for the hum of the ordinary world. You catch your reflection, in a mirror, a darkened window, a glass of something amber, and for a moment you don't recognize the face looking back. It looks like someone who never kept a promise. Then the reflection smiles, and you are not smiling.

[Gateway character's arrival — see "How they appear."]

The glass goes soft as warm wax. Cold silver closes over your fingers, your wrist, your heart. Every promise you ever whispered to a mirror plays back at once, in your own voice, a hundred times over. You fall upward through a forest of reflections: ballrooms, canals, candlelit faces in masks, a woman with a silver braid weeping over a hatbox, a man in midnight-blue falling and falling. Then rose-scented air, the roar of a crowd, and a floor of cool marble under your palms. Somewhere very close, a clock has stopped ticking. A voice in the dark says, almost fondly: "Ah. The oathless have arrived."

scenes.title: Which Gateway Character? (Roll d8)
scenes.html:
Solo: Roll once. Group: Roll once for the whole party, or have each player roll separately for a split-party opening in which everyone lands in a different place and the group reunites at the Velvet Opera by the first dawn, when Dame Ottoline's Watchmen find them by their lagging reflections.

d8 Gateway Landing point First thread
1 Lysander of the Silvered Glass Rosewater Gallery, seconds after the murder Main plot (Act I)
2 Sabine Velour The Blue Hour salon, Velvet Quarter Underworld thread: Varo, Hale, Drowned Market
3 Prince Caelum of the Dusk Edge of the Lanternwood Side Adventure 2 and the Fae endgame
4 Marisol Tidewhisper A sea cave beneath the Saltgrave Coast Side Adventure 3
5 Sir Valentin Dusk A gilded mirror in Château Dusk Side Adventure 4
6 Comic misfire: Little Gretch's hand-mirror. The shard was in an ogress's beauty kit. The PCs land in the Honeyhorn mud spa, and Gretch decides they are a gift from the gods for the Courting Moot. The Thicketmoor Side Adventure 1
7 Comic misfire: one of Vexirra's polished copper scales. The PCs land face-first in ten thousand love letters, and a dragon is very interested in where they came from. The Emberpeaks Side Adventure 5
8 Rivalry! Roll twice more (reroll 6–8). Both gateway characters reach through at once and grab a hand each. The PCs land wherever the first one leads, and the second shows up within a night, jealous and competitive. First roll's landing Both threads, plus a love triangle

Getting to the main plot from anywhere: Whatever the landing point, the Opera Council's agents (or the gateway character) bring the PCs to Dame Ottoline by the end of Night 1. Landing far from the city uses up some of Night 1 but grants a head start on that region's side adventure and its Keystone clue.

Solo entry adventures: Each of the five gateway characters has a playable solo gamebook entry adventure (levels 1–3) in the companion book Through the Oathless Glass (solo-entry-adventures.pdf). See Part 9, Solo Entry Adventures.

scenes.title: The Way Home (and Why It's Hard)
scenes.html:
The Oathless Glass opens back toward the travelers' world only at midnight, and only once the Oathless Clause is fulfilled: when a new Oathwarden has been sworn and the travelers have judged (confirmed) them with a kiss. In practice that means the way home runs through the end of the main plot, on Night 7 at the latest. Each traveler must then:

  1. Keep their mirror-promise. The promise they made to their reflection before they were pulled through must have been kept during the campaign (GM and player agree when it has been, for example "I'll be braver" kept by facing Lucan alone).
  2. Clear their Anchors. Every kiss-oath sworn in Carnelia must be fulfilled or freely released by the other party. Bargains with Caelum, dares with Marisol, and romances sealed on the lips all have to be resolved. Some will be released with a smile, and some will be released only for a price.
  3. Kiss their own reflection in the Glass and speak the kept promise aloud. The Glass softens, and they step through.

Why it's hard:

  • Everyone wants a seat. Lysander wants out, Valentin wants sunlight, Sabine wants home, and the Syndicate wants the shard so it can choose who passes. The Glass takes at most one passenger per traveler, and someone will feel betrayed.
  • The Oathwarden's chain. If a PC becomes Oathwarden (Ending C), the office binds them to Carnelia. They can't go home while they hold it, unless they freely pass the office on to someone else.
  • If the Accord fails (Ending D), the Fae Duke claims the Glass along with the city. The only way home then lies through his court in the Feywild, which makes for a whole new campaign.
  • Reflection Drift. Travelers who linger past the seventh bell without keeping their promise leave a reflection behind forever. They can still go home, but their reflection will be seen at Vesperine's masquerades for years.
  • Choosing to stay. Some travelers won't want to leave. That is a perfectly good ending. The Glass will remember them, and their reflection will smile when they look into it.

After going home: A traveler who returns keeps a small shard of the Glass. Once a year, at midnight, it shows Vesperine, and anyone who swore them a kiss-oath can wave back.

sessions.title: The Black Kiss — The Central Mystery
sessions.summary: The murder of Oathwarden Aurelian Sable at the Velvet Opera, the seven-night clock, the suspects, the clue trail and the riddles.

scenes.title: The Victim: Lord Aurelian Sable, Oathwarden of Vesperine
scenes.html:
Age 58. Silver at the temples, a dimpled smile that has ended three marriages (none of them his), always in midnight-blue velvet. Aurelian was beloved in public — generous, witty, the best dancer at any ball — and feared in private, because the man who keeps the Ledger knows every promise everyone has ever broken. He was engaged to Lady Celestine Morrow, kept the diva Seraphine Lark as his "muse," and had held the office of Oathwarden for thirty years.

How he was found. At the stroke of midnight on the Night of Unmasking, by tradition, the Oathwarden kisses the reigning star of the Opera on the Rosewater balcony as the whole house unmasks. Aurelian kissed Seraphine Lark, staggered, clawed at his mask, and fell dead by the chaise. His lips and the skin beneath his mask were stained black as Ledger ink. The crowd screamed one word: poison kiss.

scenes.title: The Truth (GM Eyes Only)
scenes.html:
The killer is Madame Thessaly Rook, the beloved maskmaker — who is secretly Lady Isaveth Sable, Aurelian's first wife.

Thirty-one years ago, Isaveth was the heiress of House Sable, one of the city's founding families, whose blood is bound to the Accord. She fell for a handsome, penniless apprentice of the Hall of Vows named Aurel Fenn. At their wedding she kissed him and swore the traditional, romantic vow: "Everything I am is yours."

Aurel knew the Ledger's ink better than anyone. He used his apprentice's access to have the Ledger read her vow literally. Overnight, her name, her title, her inheritance, and her very memory of herself transferred to him. He became "Aurelian Sable," the grieving widower of a bride "lost to the sea." She woke on the Lanternside docks with no name, no past, and a wedding ring she couldn't explain. An old maskmaker took her in. She became Thessaly Rook — and spent thirty years making masks for the man who stole her face.

Six months ago, Varo Kestrel of the Thorn Syndicate stole a page from Aurelian's private desk as blackmail material: the original wedding-vow page, which Aurelian had secretly cut out of the Ledger decades ago. The Syndicate fence, Old Mother Brine, didn't understand what it was and sold it as "antique vellum" to a lady in a grey veil buying lace for masks. When Thessaly touched the page that held her own vow, every memory came back at once.

The method. Thessaly made Aurelian's festival mask, as she had every year for thirty years.

  1. She obtained Widow's Sigh — a fey moth-orchid toxin, inert until it meets the scent of bloodrose — from the Moth Court of the Lanternwood, paying with her dream of her own wedding day.
  2. She knew Seraphine always wears Ezren Vos's bloodrose perfume, and that Aurelian would kiss Seraphine at midnight.
  3. She sabotaged the ribbon of Aurelian's festival mask so that it would fray during the evening. At 11:45, as she'd planned, Aurelian sent for her to fix it.
  4. At 11:47, she slipped through the secret door behind the mirror wall from the Dressing Gallery and swapped his mask for an identical one lined with Widow's Sigh. Brushing past, her skirts caught the long pendulum of the gallery clock beside the mirror wall — stopping it at 11:47 — and her mask-ribbon snagged on the rose trellis.
  5. At midnight, Seraphine's bloodrose-scented kiss and breath activated the toxin in the mask's lining. The black stain spread from beneath the mask, not from his lips.
  6. She stashed the original, unpoisoned mask in a costume trunk in the Dressing Gallery, meaning to collect it after the chaos. She hasn't managed it yet.

Motive. Revenge — and restoration. With Aurelian dead and the Ledger keeperless, the Accord demands a new Oathwarden of founding blood within seven nights. Isaveth intends to step forward, prove who she is with the vow-page, and reclaim her name, House, and fortune. She does not intend for the city to fall — but she underestimated how fast the oaths would unravel, and she's frightened.

What she wants from the PCs. At first: to steer them toward Celestine (who had motive and bought "poison"). Later, if exposed: their help to be named Oathwarden. She is the GM's most dangerous, most sympathetic NPC.

scenes.title: The Clock: Seven Nights of Unravelling
scenes.html:
Each night without an Oathwarden, roll on or choose from this table — the city becomes stranger and more desperate, raising stakes and creating chaos for scenes.

Night The Unravelling
1 Minor oaths fail. Gambling debts erase themselves; a dozen card-salon brawls erupt.
2 Love-vows weaken. Couples across the Gilded Crescent wake up and wonder why exactly they married each other. Comic and tragic in equal measure.
3 Trade contracts fail. Bread prices triple; the Syndicate profits. Riots in Lanternside.
4 Old curses, held at bay by protective oaths, slip free. Ghosts walk the Cypress Isle cemetery.
5 The Fae Duke's heralds — beautiful, smiling, antlered — appear at dusk, asking politely who will pay.
6 The masks of Vesperine begin to stick to their wearers' faces. Panic.
7 At midnight, the Accord fails. Unless a new Oathwarden is sworn, the Fae Duke claims the city's founding bloodlines (and their city) as his debt.

scenes.title: The Investigator's Warrant
scenes.html: The Opera Council's spokesperson, Dame Ottoline Graves (an elderly, terrifyingly polite patron with a lorgnette), hires the PCs because they are outsiders with no oaths sworn in the city — "the only people in Vesperine with nothing to hide." (If the PCs came through the Oathless Glass, this is literal: the Council's charter requires an oathless judge to confirm the next Oathwarden. See Part 2.) The Red Ribbon Warrant grants entry to any house and the right to question anyone once. Reward: 500 ducats each, plus a favor of the Council (a kiss-oath — naturally).

scenes.title: The Suspects
scenes.html:
Running the suspects. Each suspect has a flirt angle — how they use charm, and how charm works on them. A successful Persuasion (Charm) check against their DC, done with roleplay that fits their angle, unlocks their "softened" answers. Pressing with evidence (or Intimidation, or Insight to catch a lie) unlocks "under pressure." Romantic subplots are welcome between consenting adults; any intimate scene fades to black and resumes the next morning.

  • 1. Seraphine Lark — The Diva
  • 2. Lady Celestine Morrow — The Fiancée
  • 3. Captain Dorian Hale — The Watchman
  • 4. Ezren Vos — The Perfumer
  • 5. Varo Kestrel — The Fixer
  • 6. Madame Thessaly Rook — The Maskmaker (The Killer)

Full suspect profiles (appearance, flirt angle, secret, alibi, what they reveal under pressure) are in the NPCs tab.

scenes.title: The Clue Trail
scenes.html:
The PCs need any three "Keystone" clues (marked ★ below; the side adventures offer four more) to make a solid accusation of Thessaly. Each location also offers red herrings and leads to other places. No single clue is required — there are ten Keystones across the campaign, and the truth can be reached by many roads.

Location Clues found DC / Method Points toward
Rosewater Gallery (murder scene) ★ Clock stopped at 11:47 (Riddle 6 on its case reveals the pendulum was knocked, not wound down). Lavender silk mask-ribbon snagged on the trellis by the mirror wall. The black stain is darkest under where the mask sat, faint on the lips. Investigation DC 12 (ribbon), Medicine DC 14 (stain pattern) Someone came through the mirror door before midnight; the poison was in the mask
Dressing Gallery (behind mirror wall) ★ The original, unpoisoned mask of Aurelian, hidden in a costume trunk — its ribbon cut, not frayed. Actors' testimony: Thessaly "stepped out around quarter to." Investigation DC 14, or Persuasion DC 12 with the actors Masks were swapped; Thessaly left her station
Sable Palazzo (study) Riddle-locked desk (Riddle 1): Aurelian's journal — "The masks remember. She cannot. She must not." — and the faceless porcelain mask sent to him anonymously. A painted-over portrait in the gallery (scrape it or use detect magic): a young bride with Thessaly's eyes. Riddle; Investigation DC 15 for the portrait Aurelian had a secret involving a woman he wronged
Vos Perfumery Widow's Sigh identification. ★ Coded order ledger (Riddle 3): "Madame R. — bloodrose, 1 vial." Oath-breaking salts order for "Lady C.M." (red herring). Riddle; Ezren's cooperation Thessaly tested the poison; Celestine looks guilty
Drowned Market (Mother Brine) Password riddle (Riddle 5). Mother Brine's sale record: "Old vellum page, wedding oath, sold to lady in grey veil for 3 masks." ★ One of the three masks, still on display — signed inside with Thessaly's maker's mark. Riddle; Persuasion DC 13 or 20 ducats The vow-page went to Thessaly
Hall of Vows / Vault of Broken Vows Vault door riddle (Riddle 2); needs Varo's key or Thieves' Tools DC 18. Inside: the Ledger, bleeding ink; a missing page stub dated 31 years ago with surviving text: "…Aurel Fenn and Isaveth Sable, everything I am…" The Veiled Sisters confirm that a vow-page touched by its swearer restores what it holds. Riddle + access; History DC 13 Aurelian stole his wife's identity
Sable Crypt (Cypress Isle) Riddle 4 on the sarcophagus. ★ The tomb of "Lady Isaveth Sable" is empty, except for a wedding veil of lavender silk matching the ribbon in the Gallery. Ghosts (Night 4+) whisper "she lives, she sews, she smiles." Riddle; Athletics DC 15 to open the lid otherwise Isaveth is alive; lavender links to Thessaly
Thessaly's Atelier (Search with a warrant or by stealth.) A hatbox holding a thirty-year-old wedding mask and ★ the vow-page itself, wrapped in lavender silk. A pressed moth-orchid in a book of poems. Investigation DC 16 or Stealth DC 15 to search unseen Proof of identity and motive; the orchid points to the Lanternwood
The Lanternwood (side quest) Queen Ilysse of the Moth Court will reveal (if bargained with) that "a silver-haired woman traded the dream of her wedding day for a sigh of our orchid." See Side Adventure 2 Confirms Thessaly obtained the poison

Speak with Dead & truth magic. Aurelian's corpse answers honestly but knows little: "I kissed her and I burned" (misleads toward Seraphine); "The masks remember"; if asked about his wife: "Everything she was is mine." Zone of truth works normally, but Thessaly answers only literal questions literally ("Were you in the Dressing Gallery all evening?" "I was in and around it, yes, darling.").

scenes.title: Red Herrings
scenes.html:
1. The Poison Kiss. Everyone believes Seraphine's kiss killed him. It did — but only as the trigger.
  2. Celestine's "Poison." The white crystals in her vanity are fake oath-breaking salts. The burned love letter makes her look like a conspirator.
  3. Hale's Purse. A Syndicate bribe — real corruption, unrelated to murder.
  4. Varo's Stolen Key. He was caught robbing the corpse's coat — a thief, not a killer.
  5. Dream-Moth Dust. Traces of dream-moth dust on Aurelian's collar point to the Lanternwood and the Moth Court. He used it recreationally. (But following it to the Lanternwood does uncover the orchid trade.)
  6. The Syndicate Frame. On Night 3, the Thorn Syndicate plants a forged letter signed "S." in Seraphine's dressing room ("It will be done at midnight") to keep her pliable. A DC 15 Investigation check spots the forgery (the ink is fresh; Seraphine signs with a little lark doodle, not a letter).

scenes.title: The Riddles of the Black Kiss
scenes.html:
Running riddles. Read the riddle aloud and give the players time. If they're stuck, allow an Intelligence (Investigation) or Wisdom (Insight) check (DC 13) for a hint; a failed check still gives the hint, but costs time (advance the night by one scene) or attracts trouble.

Riddle 1 — Aurelian's Desk (a brass lock shaped like lips; speak the answer to it)

Carved to smile, I cannot laugh;
I wear no face, yet I am half
of every lie the dancers tell.
Lift me, love, and break the spell.

Answer: A mask. Hint: "What does every dancer in Vesperine wear tonight?"

Riddle 2 — The Vault of Broken Vows (carved above the door; a Veiled Sister asks it)

Given freely, I weigh nothing;
broken, I'm as heavy as stone.
Lips make me, lies unmake me,
and I am never wholly your own.

Answer: A promise (an oath / a vow). Hint: "What is this whole hall full of?"

Riddle 3 — Ezren's Scent-Coded Ledger (the cipher key on the first page)

I arrive before the lover
and linger when she's gone.
You cannot see or hold me,
yet I swear where she has been.

Answer: A scent (perfume). Saying "scent" lets the reader realize each customer is recorded under the name of a scent. Ezren's code-names: Lavender = Madame Rook; Frost-Lily = Lady Celestine; Bloodrose = Seraphine. The page reads: "Lavender — 1 vial bloodrose."

Riddle 4 — The Empty Sarcophagus (inscribed on the lid of Isaveth's tomb)

What can be stolen, yet never be touched,
lost while you hold it, and taken with a kiss —
and returned to its owner only by being spoken?

Answer: A name. Speaking "a name" — or speaking "Isaveth" — slides the lid open. Hint: "What's carved above every tomb?"

Riddle 5 — Mother Brine's Password (she asks it through a slot in her door)

I have leaves but no branches,
a spine but no bones;
I hold a thousand kisses
and I've never been kissed.

Answer: A book (the Ledger). Hint: "What does every scholar and lover in the Hall of Vows keep their eyes on?"

Riddle 6 — The Gallery Clock (engraved on its glass case; solving it lets the PCs open the case without breaking the enchantment protecting it)

I have a face but cannot see,
two hands but cannot hold.
I strike, but I wound no one;
stop my heart and I grow cold —
yet the moment of my dying
is the truth I've always told.

Answer: A clock. Inside, the pendulum is bent sideways and caught with a strand of lavender silk — knocked, not wound down. The stopped time, 11:47, is the moment someone came through the mirror door.

sessions.title: Side Adventure 1 — The Courting Moot of the Honeyhorn Matrons
sessions.summary: Region: The Thicketmoor · Levels: 3–5 · Faction: The Honeyhorn Clan (ogresses)

scenes.title: About this adventure
scenes.html:
Region: The Thicketmoor · Levels: 3–5 · Faction: The Honeyhorn Clan (ogresses) Tone: Danger plus bawdy comedy. Think a sitcom with a body count that could happen.

Each side adventure belongs to a distinct faction, contains a dungeon outline, a riddle or puzzle, and at least four resolution paths. Each also feeds the main mystery with an alternate clue, an ally, or leverage — so players who wander off are rewarded, not punished.

Time cost: Each side adventure takes roughly one night on the Unravelling clock (travel by fast horse or boat, an evening's adventure, return by dawn). Players who go on every side quest will be racing the seventh bell — which is exactly the right amount of pressure.

scenes.title: The Situation
scenes.html:
Men are vanishing on the Bog Causeway — a carter, two Lantern Watch recruits, a poet, and most importantly Pell Ambrose, the Velvet Opera's stage carpenter, who fled the city the morning after the murder. Pell built the mirror-wall door, and he was mending a sandbag rope backstage at 11:47. He saw Madame Rook come back through it, white as milk. He fled because he's terrified of being blamed.

The kidnappers are the Honeyhorn Matrons: a clan of six ogresses who have been without their menfolk for forty years. At their last Courting Moot, the ogre men of Honeyhorn were too proud to declare their love, and a jilted bog hag named Auntie Sallowmere cursed every one of them into a standing stone — the Sulking Stones — "until somebody finally says it."

The matrons don't know how to break the curse, and they are lonely. So every autumn they hold a new Courting Moot, kidnap "husband-candidates" from the road, and put them through courtship trials. The captives are absurdly pampered: crowned with marsh-lilies, fed enormous honey-cakes, scrubbed in the mud spa, and made to recite poetry. Courtship here is relentlessly wholesome-ridiculous — hand-holding, serenades, being carried around like a prize ham. Nothing romantic actually happens to the captives, and the captives very much want to go home.

The danger: a candidate who fails all five trials is declared a "Disappointment," and Disappointments go in the Disappointment Pot. The Moot is in two days. Pell has already failed two trials (he can't sing, and he cried during arm-wrestling).

scenes.title: Key NPCs
scenes.html:
• Big Mother Hulga Tenderbone — Clan matriarch, 10 feet tall, braids woven with bones and dried roses, an apron reading (in crude Common) KISS THE COOK. Loud, sentimental, quick to weep and quicker to smash. Secretly writes love poems to her petrified husband, Grunwald.
  • Brunhilde "Bru" — Hulga's eldest daughter. Bodybuilder energy. Flirts by arm-wrestling and lifting people over her head. Respects anyone who beats her at anything.
  • Little Gretch — The "small" one, only eight feet. Romantic, shy, reads stolen chapbook romances. Most likely to help the PCs.
  • Granny Moss — Ancient, blind, sharp-tongued, the only one who remembers exactly what the hag said. Will trade information for gossip.
  • Auntie Sallowmere — A green hag who lives beneath the bog. Petty, vain, hilarious, and still sulking after forty years.
  • The Captives — Pell Ambrose (nervous, sweet), Rufus the carter (has accepted his fate and is enjoying the cake), Watchmen Dobbs and Pirelli (in denial), and Lorcan the poet (who's frankly having the time of his life and is technically a willing guest — he walked in on purpose).

scenes.title: Dungeon: The Hive-Hall of Honeyhorn
scenes.html:
[7] SULKING STONES (outside, ring of 6 stones)
                    |
 [1] BRAMBLE GATE -- [2] THE WALLOWS -- [5] THE MOOT RING
                         |                  |
                   [3] PAMPERING PEN   [6] HULGA'S BOWER
                         |
                   [4] KITCHEN of the DISAPPOINTMENT POT
                         |
                   (sinkhole) --> [8] SALLOWMERE'S HUT (under the bog)
  1. Bramble Gate. A wall of brambles with a gate of woven thorns. Hives of honey-wasps (swarm of insects) hang overhead; a noisy approach (failed DC 13 group Stealth) drops a hive. The honey is delicious and slightly intoxicating (DC 11 Con or poisoned for 1 hour — "sweet-drunk").
  2. The Wallows. Steaming mud pits where two ogresses lounge with cucumber slices on their eyes. They'll mistake well-dressed PCs for "a delivery of new candidates." Hide in the mud for advantage on Stealth (and disadvantage on Charisma checks afterwards — you smell).
  3. The Pampering Pen. A giant willow cage strung with flowers. Captives in lily crowns. A captive will beg the PCs to rescue them, then beg them to wait until after dessert. The lock is a knot (DC 14 Dexterity with thieves' tools or DC 16 Strength to rip the willow).
  4. Kitchen of the Disappointment Pot. A cauldron big enough to bathe in, already simmering with turnips. A comedic hazard: the floor is slick with grease (DC 12 Dex or prone), the spice rack is full of ogre pepper (thrown, it blinds for 1 round). Recipe pinned to the wall: DISAPOYNTMENT STOO — 1 man (sad), 4 turnips, onyon.
  5. The Moot Ring. A trampled clearing with a judges' log and a giant heart-shaped wreath. Site of the Courting Moot trials (see Charm path).
  6. Hulga's Bower. Hulga's den: a nest of furs, forty years of love poems carved on bark, and the clan treasure (see Rewards). A stuffed bear wearing a wedding veil.
  7. The Sulking Stones. Six grey standing stones in a circle, each vaguely ogre-shaped and scowling, arms crossed. The riddle is carved into the center stone.
  8. Sallowmere's Hut. Reached through a sinkhole in the kitchen (DC 15 Perception to notice the draft). A hut on chicken-legs half-sunk in mud, decorated with forty years of wedding invitations she sent to herself. The hag fights dirty but surrenders if offered flattery, an apology, or a better grudge.

scenes.title: The Riddle of the Sulking Stones
scenes.html:
Carved in the center stone, in Giant and (badly) in Common:

We stood too proud to say it,
so we stand here proud and still.
Three words will set us walking —
if one of you has the will.
Not ours to speak; we're only stone.
Let her who loves us speak alone.

Answer: "I love you." But the trick is in the last couplet: the matrons must say it — and they are every bit as proud as their husbands. Hulga has written forty years of poems and never once said it aloud. Getting six ogresses to declare their love to rocks, sincerely, is a social puzzle (Persuasion or Performance DC 15 per matron; Gretch goes first easily, Hulga is DC 20 and needs to be the last). When the last matron speaks, the stones crack and six enormous, embarrassed ogre husbands step out — mid-sentence, forty years late.

scenes.title: Resolution Paths
scenes.html:
• Combat. Six ogres (use Hulga as an ogre with 85 HP and two Greatclub attacks; Bru has advantage on grapples). Ogres are dangerous at level 3 — encourage tactics: the Wallows are difficult terrain, the Kitchen grease, the honey-wasps can be dropped on ogres too. Winning by force earns the clan's enmity; the surviving matrons raid the Bog Causeway for revenge.
  • Charm — Win the Courting Moot. Any PC of any gender may enter as a "champion." The Moot has five trials; win three (opposed checks against a matron) and the matrons declare the champion so magnificent that all other candidates are "unworthy" and released: 1. The Hog-Hoist — Athletics vs. Bru (+6). 2. The Serenade — Performance DC 14 (ogres love tragic songs). 3. The Feast — Constitution save DC 15 to eat a whole honey-ham. 4. The Love Poem — Performance or Intelligence DC 13; bonus for the word "turnip." 5. The Mud Waltz — Acrobatics DC 14 while dancing with Hulga. The champion is then "betrothed" to Hulga. Getting out of the engagement gracefully (or breaking the curse so she can go back to Grunwald) is part of the fun. Any flirtation with a matron by a free, willing PC is fine — fade to black, and she makes breakfast for twenty.
  • Stealth — The Mud-Bath Snore. At dusk every day the whole clan takes a one-hour mud bath and falls asleep. A group Stealth check (DC 14) gets the PCs in and out; each failure wakes one ogress, who must be lulled (Performance DC 13 — a lullaby) or silenced. Rufus the carter does not want to leave without the cake.
  • Bargain — Break the Curse. Ask Granny Moss (trade gossip from Vesperine), solve the stones' riddle, and coax the matrons into confessing their love — or descend to Sallowmere and convince her to lift it (apology on behalf of the ogre men, or flattery: Persuasion DC 16). Freed husbands = the clan releases all captives and becomes staunch allies of the PCs.

scenes.title: Rewards & Ties to the Main Plot
scenes.html:
• Pell Ambrose's testimony: "At about quarter to midnight, I saw Madame Rook come back through the mirror door with a mask under her shawl. She looked at me like she'd seen a ghost." — counts as a Keystone clue.
  • Hulga's clan treasure: 300 gp in mixed coins, a potion of giant strength (hill), and a jar of Honeyhorn mead (drink: advantage on one Charisma check, and you will sing).
  • Allies: If the curse is broken, the Honeyhorn ogres will stomp into Vesperine on Night 7 to help defend the city (see Endings).

sessions.title: Side Adventure 2 — The Dreamthieves of the Moth Court
sessions.summary: Region: The Lanternwood · Levels: 4–6 · Faction: The Moth Court (fey)

scenes.title: About this adventure
scenes.html: Region: The Lanternwood · Levels: 4–6 · Faction: The Moth Court (fey) Tone: Dreamy, languid, sensual danger. Velvet wings, whispered bargains.

scenes.title: The Situation
scenes.html:
Across Vesperine, people are falling into enchanted sleep, smiling, dusted with silver moth-powder. Among them is Teodor Graves, Dame Ottoline's beloved grandson — and the Council will grant the PCs extra time (one extra night on the clock) if he's saved.

The Moth Court of the Lanternwood — tall, pale fey with soft, feathered antennae and wings patterned like eyes — feed on dreams. Since the Accord began to unravel, the old treaty that limited their harvest has weakened, and Queen Ilysse of the Hush has been gorging. She is not cruel, exactly. She is hungry and bored, and she adores beautiful things.

Tie to the mystery: The Moth Court supplies the rare moth-orchid from which Widow's Sigh is made. Ilysse remembers the silver-haired woman who bought it; she paid with her dream of her own wedding day — which the Queen keeps in a cocoon in her Silk Library. Viewing it shows young Isaveth Sable marrying a young Aurel Fenn — a Keystone clue.

scenes.title: Key NPCs
scenes.html:
• Queen Ilysse of the Hush — Wings of dusky violet and gold, eyes like wet ink, a gown that seems spun of moonlight. Speaks in a near-whisper so you must lean close. Seductive in the manner of something ancient and amused. Collects compliments, dances, and truths.
  • Sir Fennic Ashwing — Her champion and consort, jealous, theatrical, a skilled duelist who challenges anyone the Queen smiles at.
  • The Dust-Maidens — Attendants who scatter sleep-pollen and giggle a lot.
  • Teodor Graves — A sleeping young nobleman wrapped in silk in the Library, dreaming of being a famous sailor.

scenes.title: Dungeon: The Cocoon Palace
scenes.html:
1. The Avenue of Lights. A path of glowing trees and drifting lights — some of them will-o'-wisps that lure travellers toward a sinkhole of sleep-pollen. Insight DC 14 tells real fey-lights from hungry ones.
  2. The Dust Fields. Silver pollen drifts like snow. DC 13 Constitution save each 10 minutes or fall asleep for 1 minute (and have one vivid, embarrassing dream, which the Dust-Maidens witness and gossip about later). Cloth masks give advantage.
  3. The Hall of Wings. Ten-foot moths (use giant wasp stats, no poison; their wings cause blindness on a hit, DC 12 Con) guard the palace gate. They can be soothed with lantern-light in a rhythmic pattern (Animal Handling DC 14).
  4. The Mirror Pool. A still pool that shows each viewer their heart's desire. DC 15 Wisdom save or be charmed and stand gazing for an hour. A charmed PC can be pulled free by an ally speaking a true, kind thing about them.
  5. The Silk Library. Thousands of silken cocoons hang from the ceiling like lanterns, each humming with a stolen dream. The puzzle (below) helps find the right ones.
  6. The Hush Throne. A throne of living moths in a hall of silver birches. Revels every night: music, wine that tastes like memory, dancing.

scenes.title: Puzzle: The Silk Library
scenes.html:
Each cocoon bears a silken tag with a riddle-name. A Dust-Maiden recites the librarian's rhyme:

I am the feast you never eat,
the kiss you never feel,
the road you walk on sleeping feet,
and lose when you grow real.

Answer: A dream. Answering grants the "librarian's courtesy": the cocoons will hum louder when a seeker names the dreamer. Naming Teodor Graves finds him; naming Isaveth Sable finds the wedding dream (naming "Thessaly Rook" finds nothing — a clue in itself).

scenes.title: Resolution Paths
scenes.html:
• Combat. Queen Ilysse (use the mage stat block with 75 HP, fey ancestry, and sleep at 5th level as a recharge 5–6 ability), Sir Fennic (gladiator with flying), and 2–4 giant moths. Killing the Queen releases all dreams — but her court flees in grief and the Lanternwood goes dark; the orchid trade, and the Court's testimony, are lost.
  • Charm — Dance the Moth Waltz. Join the revels. Three rounds of dancing (Performance or Acrobatics DC 14), each paired with offering the Queen a compliment she hasn't heard in a hundred years (Persuasion DC 15; inventive roleplay grants advantage). Win her favor and she releases Teodor as "a party favor." Sir Fennic will demand a duel of honor afterward (first blood). A PC who catches the Queen's eye may be invited to stay after the revels — fade to black; they wake at dawn on a bed of moss with a moth-wing cloak (as a cloak of elvenkind) and their dreams a little brighter.
  • Stealth — The Dimming. For one hour before dawn, the court sleeps, wings folded. A group Stealth check (DC 15) through the Dust Fields and Hall of Wings lets the PCs cut down cocoons. Each cut cocoon releases a dream as a little burst of light and sound — someone always cuts a loud one.
  • Bargain — A Dream for a Dream. The Queen will trade: Teodor's dream (and the wedding dream) for one dream from a PC. The PC permanently loses a happy memory of the player's choosing (roleplay it), but gains the Queen's token: one free dream spell cast by the Court on their behalf.

scenes.title: Rewards & Ties
scenes.html:
• The wedding dream (Keystone clue) and the Queen's testimony.
  • Teodor saved: +1 night on the Unravelling clock (the Council buys time with the Fae heralds).
  • Moth-orchid sample (Ezren can confirm it's the source of Widow's Sigh).
  • Treasure: 4 potions of healing in moonlit glass, a moth-wing cloak (via the Charm path), 250 gp in moonstones.

sessions.title: Side Adventure 3 — The Song Beneath Saltgrave
sessions.summary: Region: The Saltgrave Coast · Levels: 5–7 · Factions: The Drowned Choir (sirens) and the Thorn Syndicate (smugglers)

scenes.title: About this adventure
scenes.html: Region: The Saltgrave Coast · Levels: 5–7 · Factions: The Drowned Choir (sirens) and the Thorn Syndicate (smugglers) Tone: Salt, storms, piracy, and voices that pull you overboard.

scenes.title: The Situation
scenes.html:
Ships are wrecking on the Saltgrave cliffs every night, lured by song. The Lantern Watch blames the Drowned Choir, a sisterhood of merfolk sirens who have lived peaceably in the sea caves for centuries. The truth: Captain Morven "Saltlick" Kray, the Thorn Syndicate's chief smuggler, has stolen the Pearl Heart — the shell that holds the Choir's true voices — and is forcing them to sing ships to ruin so his wreckers can loot the cargo.

Tie to the mystery: The Syndicate keeps its blackmail archive in Kray's strongroom: proof of Captain Hale's debts (leverage to make him cooperate), and Varo's original report describing the stolen vow-page ("'Aurel Fenn & Isaveth Sable' — sold by Brine to grey-veil lady, Needle Row"). The archive also holds dirt on half the Opera Council — a powerful bargaining chip in the endgame.

scenes.title: Key NPCs
scenes.html:
• Mother-of-Pearl Nerissa — Choir leader, silver-scaled, hair like kelp in moonlight, voice now a hoarse whisper. Proud, furious, irresistibly charismatic even voiceless.
  • Captain Morven "Saltlick" Kray — Human, one eye, tattooed knuckles reading SALT / LICK, a grin full of gold teeth. Flirts by insulting you. Uses the bandit captain stat block (+20 HP).
  • Quill-Fin — A young merfolk siren who'll guide the PCs through the underwater ways in exchange for a kiss on the cheek (she's an adult and does this to everyone as a dare; it seals a small oath of guidance under the Accord).
  • The Wreckers — Bandits and thugs with lanterns and hooked poles.

scenes.title: Dungeon: The Smugglers' Grotto
scenes.html:
1. The Wrecker's Beacon. A false lighthouse on the cliff. Douse it (stealth) or hold it (combat vs. 4 bandits). From here a stair descends into the cliff.
  2. The Tidepool Stair. A slick, winding stair half-flooded at high tide. A tide timer: every 10 minutes in the grotto, the water rises a level. After 30 minutes, the lower rooms are underwater.
  3. The Syndicate Warehouse. Crates of wrecked cargo, rum, silk — and a crate of Vos's fake oath-breaking salts. 6 thugs playing dice. Bribable, drunk, or gullible (Deception DC 13: "Kray sent us").
  4. The Drowned Chapel. An ancient sea-temple, half-flooded, with the song-lock door (see Puzzle). Beyond it is the only route to the Choir Lagoon that doesn't pass Kray.
  5. The Choir Lagoon. A vast, moonlit cave lagoon. The sirens sing in chains of enchanted coral — their stolen song forced from them by the Pearl Heart. DC 14 Wisdom save each round of music or move toward the water. Freeing the Choir silences it.
  6. Kray's Strongroom. A ship's cabin wedged into the rock. The Pearl Heart sits in a locked iron box (DC 17 thieves' tools; the key is on Kray). The blackmail archive is in a sea-chest.

scenes.title: Puzzle: The Song-Lock of the Drowned Chapel
scenes.html:
Five carved shells protrude from the chapel door: a gull, a bell, a wave, a wind-face, and a heart. Each sings a note when pressed. The inscription reads:

First the gull, who cries for none;
then the bell that tolls the drowned;
then the wave that breaks, the wind that lies,
and last, the heart that makes no sound.

Solution: Press gull, bell, wave, wind, then press and hold the heart — while the whole party stays utterly silent for one round (the heart "makes no sound"). Any speech, spell with a verbal component, or clanking armor (Stealth DC 12 for heavy armor) resets the lock and rings a bell that alerts the warehouse.

scenes.title: Resolution Paths
scenes.html:
• Combat. Storm the grotto: Kray, his first mate (veteran), and 8 bandits/thugs. Fight while the tide rises and the sirens' forced song charms combatants on both sides.
  • Charm. Kray is vain and lonely. A PC who out-insults him (opposed Charisma (Deception or Performance) — he loves a sharp tongue) and drinks him under the table (Constitution DC 15, three rounds) can talk him into "showing off" the Pearl Heart. Or seduce his first mate, Bel Okafor, who hates Kray and is looking for an excuse (and, if both are willing, a dalliance — fade to black, she wakes up with a plan).
  • Stealth. Use Quill-Fin's underwater passages (requires water breathing or holding breath — DC 12 Con per 2 minutes) to reach the Drowned Chapel, solve the song-lock, slip into the strongroom, and steal the Pearl Heart.
  • Bargain. Offer Kray a better deal: Varo, Hale, or the PCs' Red Ribbon Warrant can promise him a pardon, or the PCs can threaten to expose him to the Syndicate's boss (Mother Brine), whom he is skimming from.

scenes.title: Rewards & Ties
scenes.html:
• Returning the Pearl Heart: the Choir's eternal friendship. Nerissa sings one Song of Calling for the PCs — on Night 7, the Choir can drown out the Fae Duke's heralds' fey-music, giving all allies advantage on saves against charm.
  • Blackmail archive: leverage over Hale (he'll cooperate fully), over the Opera Council (one free vote in the endgame), and Varo's report (supporting clue).
  • Treasure: 600 gp in salvaged goods, a trident of fish command, a cap of water breathing.

sessions.title: Side Adventure 4 — The Crimson Vintage
sessions.summary: Region: The Duskvine Valley · Levels: 6–8 · Faction: House Dusk (vampire nobility) and its thralls

scenes.title: About this adventure
scenes.html: Region: The Duskvine Valley · Levels: 6–8 · Faction: House Dusk (vampire nobility) and its thralls Tone: Gothic glamour. Candlelight, decadence, and something hungry in the cellar.

scenes.title: The Situation
scenes.html:
Villagers of the Duskvine have been disappearing for weeks. Everyone blames Countess Morwenna Dusk, the valley's reclusive vintner — and a member of the Opera Council, whose vote will matter on Night 7. Everyone suspects she is a vampire. Everyone is right.

But Morwenna is a civilized monster. For two centuries she has fed only on willing, well-paid donors at her famous Harvest Masquerades, and lives otherwise on her legendary Crimson Vintage. The disappearances are the work of her steward and spawn, Lucan Vey, who has been turning stolen villagers into a secret army. He plans to destroy Morwenna and seize her vote, so the Syndicate can install its puppet as Oathwarden.

Tie to the mystery: Morwenna knew Isaveth Sable as a child; she attended Isaveth's wedding 31 years ago. If she meets Thessaly, she will recognize her instantly — a living witness to the identity (a Keystone clue). She also controls a vote in the endgame.

scenes.title: Key NPCs
scenes.html:
• Countess Morwenna Dusk — Tall, raven-haired, gown of black and wine-red velvet, lips like a fresh cut. Witty, melancholy, devastatingly flirtatious in a slow, old-world way. She flirts with everyone but feeds only on the willing — and says so, crisply, to anyone who assumes otherwise. Use the vampire stat block if it ever comes to that (it shouldn't, if the PCs are smart).
  • Lucan Vey — Her steward. Handsome, golden, polite to a fault. Ambitious beyond reason. Vampire spawn with 110 HP and Legendary Resistance (1/day).
  • Marta Ilic — A sharp-eyed village innkeeper whose son vanished; she's the PCs' contact.
  • The Donors — Well-dressed adults who attend the masquerade willingly and boast about it like a spa visit.

scenes.title: Dungeon: Château Dusk & the Deep Cellars
scenes.html:
1. The Grand Tasting Hall. The Harvest Masquerade: candlelit, musicians, gorgeous guests, the Countess receiving admirers on a velvet divan. A social stage — Insight DC 15 notices the servants' fear of Lucan, not of the Countess.
  2. The Pressing Room. An enormous enchanted grape-press, animated by Lucan to guard the cellar stair (use animated armor ×2, or a shambling mound reskinned as a press of crushed vines). Floors slick with must (difficult terrain).
  3. The Barrel Labyrinth. A maze of thousand-year-old casks. Light sources go out mysteriously (Lucan's spawn). Navigation: Survival DC 14 or follow the faint smell of fresh, not aged, blood (Perception DC 13).
  4. The Vintage Vault. Morwenna's private reserve, sealed by a riddle-lock (below). Inside: ancient bottles, family records — and her diary entry from Isaveth's wedding.
  5. Lucan's Crypt-Chapel. A deconsecrated chapel where captive villagers are held in iron cages, pale and dazed but alive. Four vampire spawn (newly turned) guard them. Lucan's coffin rests behind the altar.
  6. The Sunroof Tower. The château's old observatory — a great brass shutter that, once opened at dawn, floods the crypt-chapel below with sunlight through a shaft. A clockwork puzzle (Intelligence DC 15, or brute force: Strength DC 18).

scenes.title: Riddle: The Vintage Vault
scenes.html:
Engraved on a silver plate above a lock shaped like a bunch of grapes:

I'm born of crushing, laid to sleep in the dark;
the longer I'm buried, the brighter my spark.
I loosen your tongue and I loosen your laces —
I'm blood in the chalice of holy places.

Answer: Wine. (Speak it, or pour wine over the grape-lock.)

scenes.title: Resolution Paths
scenes.html:
• Combat. Descend to the crypt-chapel and fight Lucan and his spawn — ideally at dawn, with the Sunroof Tower opened, which deals 10 (3d6) radiant damage per round to every vampire in the shaft.
  • Charm. Win the Countess's trust at the masquerade (Persuasion DC 16, or present proof of Lucan's crimes). A PC who flirts with her as an equal gets her fascinated attention; she may invite a willing PC to her private salon — strictly a fade to black, and she is scrupulous about consent. As an ally, she confronts Lucan herself (a spectacular vampire duel in the cellars).
  • Stealth. Slip away from the masquerade, navigate the Barrel Labyrinth, free the villagers, and escape before Lucan notices (group Stealth DC 15, then a chase through the vineyards).
  • Bargain. Lucan offers the PCs a share in the coming Syndicate "new order" and the Council vote if they'll help him kill Morwenna. Accepting (or pretending to) puts the PCs on a very dark path — and Lucan will betray them on Night 7.

scenes.title: Rewards & Ties
scenes.html:
• Morwenna's diary entry and testimony identifying Thessaly as Isaveth — Keystone clue.
  • Morwenna's Council vote in the endgame.
  • Treasure: a crate of Crimson Vintage (worth 500 gp, and a fine bribe anywhere), a ring of protection, a rapier +1 named Last Toast.

sessions.title: Side Adventure 5 — A Hoard of Love Letters
sessions.summary: Region: The Emberpeaks · Levels: 6–8 · Factions: Vexirra the copper dragon; the Copperhand Miners' Guild; the Inkscale Troupe (kobold poets)

scenes.title: About this adventure
scenes.html: Region: The Emberpeaks · Levels: 6–8 · Factions: Vexirra the copper dragon; the Copperhand Miners' Guild; the Inkscale Troupe (kobold poets) Tone: Romantic comedy with a dragon. Steam, wit, and a very real chance of being set on fire... well, acid-sprayed.

scenes.title: The Situation
scenes.html:
Every love letter in Vesperine has stopped arriving. Couriers on the Copper Road are being snatched — not their gold, just their mailbags. The culprit is Vexirra, a young copper dragon who lives among the hot springs of the Emberpeaks and has started hoarding love letters because she has never received one. She reads them aloud to her kobolds and weeps.

The Copperhand Miners' Guild (dwarves and gnomes) want her gone because her kobolds keep stealing their copper wire to bind letters into books, and have posted a bounty. The Inkscale Troupe of kobold poet-servants adore her and will die for her (dramatically, in verse).

Tie to the mystery: One of the mailbags held Aurelian Sable's last letter, sent the week before his death to his lawyer: "I believe Isaveth has remembered. If I die, look to the woman who makes my face." — a Keystone clue straight from the victim's hand.

scenes.title: Key NPCs
scenes.html:
• Vexirra — A young copper dragon (CR 7) with scales like a new penny, a talent for impressions, and terrible taste in jokes. Insists she is an "adult" dragon. Desperately romantic, prickly when embarrassed. Can polymorph-style disguise herself as a red-haired human woman with freckles and copper-rimmed spectacles (a feature of this world's copper dragons) — she sometimes goes to the city this way, too shy to talk to anyone.
  • Scribbletail — The kobold chief poet. Writes appalling sonnets. Jealous of anyone the dragon likes.
  • Forewoman Brannagh Copperhand — Dwarven guild boss: grizzled, practical, secretly a romantic who writes letters to her late husband and burns them.

scenes.title: Dungeon: The Lair of Steam & Paper
scenes.html:
1. The Sky-Bridge. A swaying rope bridge across a steaming chasm. Winds gust (DC 13 Dex or slip; rope tie-offs grant advantage). Kobold lookouts ring a bell.
  2. The Kobold Scriptorium. A cave of tiny desks where kobolds copy love letters into bound books by candlelight. 10 kobolds (and 2 winged kobolds). They can be fought, flattered, or out-poeted (Performance DC 12).
  3. The Hot-Spring Galleries. Terraced springs and thick steam (heavily obscured). A stealthy route, but the steam muffles sound — and slick stones (DC 12 Acrobatics) hide scalding pools (2d6 fire damage).
  4. The Echo Hall. A cavern of echoes that only lets you pass if you answer its riddle (below). Speak wrongly and the echo becomes a deafening shriek (DC 13 Con or 2d6 thunder damage and deafened for 1 minute).
  5. The Hoard of Letters. A cavern heaped with ten thousand letters, a little copper and gold mixed in. Fire hazard: any fire spell here sets the hoard ablaze — and Vexirra will never, ever forgive you.
  6. Vexirra's Bath. A huge copper-lined hot spring where the dragon soaks, reading. The best place to talk to her. The worst place to fight her (she has the high ground and the boiling water).

scenes.title: Riddle: The Echo Hall
scenes.html:
The echo whispers in a dozen voices:

I grow bigger the more that I'm shared,
I burn without any fire;
I'm lighter when carried by two who have dared,
and heaviest kept by a liar.

Answer: Love. (Accept "a secret" as a clever alternate answer — the echo laughs and lets you pass, but warns Vexirra you're coming.)

scenes.title: Resolution Paths
scenes.html:
• Combat. Vexirra (young copper dragon) plus kobolds. She fights evasively, spits acid, uses slowing breath, and flees to the sky if losing — then raids the Copper Road in revenge for weeks. Combat in the Hoard risks burning the key letter.
  • Charm — Write Her a Love Letter. Vexirra will release the mail (and the mailbags) to anyone who writes her a letter that makes her cry. Have the player actually write a short one (or roll Performance DC 17, with advantage for genuinely heartfelt roleplay at the table). She may want a date — a PC who's willing can take her (in human form) to the Opera; fade to black, and she becomes the party's devoted friend for life.
  • Stealth. Sneak through the Hot-Spring Galleries while she bathes, search the hoard for the right mailbag (Investigation DC 15; each failed check takes 10 minutes — and kobolds patrol every 20).
  • Bargain — Find Her a Pen-Pal. Broker a correspondence. Forewoman Brannagh secretly writes beautiful letters; or (comedy gold) introduce Vexirra to Big Mother Hulga's lovesick daughter Gretch as a fellow romance-reader. If the PCs promise her real letters, she returns all the mail and calls off her kobolds; the Miners' Guild pays the bounty anyway.

scenes.title: Rewards & Ties
scenes.html:
• Aurelian's last letter — Keystone clue.
  • Miners' Guild bounty: 800 gp. Vexirra's gift: a wand of magic missiles she uses as a letter-opener, and one Copper Scale (once, the bearer can cast calm emotions).
  • Ally: Vexirra will fly to Vesperine on Night 7 if the party is her friend — dragonback rescue or dramatic entrance.

sessions.title: The Fair Folk — Tempters, Tricksters & Thorns
sessions.summary: The fey courts, the Enthrallment track, the Thornwake ballroom and the fey endgame.

scenes.title: Introduction
scenes.html:
"Never thank them. Never give your name. Never eat the honey. And if one of them kisses you — darling, check your pockets, your purse, and your soul, in that order." — Vesperine nursery rhyme, recited in salons as a drinking game

The Accord of Lips was struck with the fey, so the fey have always been close to Carnelia. Their nearness grows as the Accord unravels. This part expands the fey of the Velvet Marches into a full faction web, with two kinds of fey:

  • Tempters are pixies, sprites, nymphs, and satyrs who flirt, lure, and trick for the sheer fun of it. Mischievous rather than malicious, they can become allies, informants, or delightful nuisances.
  • Thorns are dark fey who use seduction as a leash: glamours, enchanted kisses, kiss-bound vows, addictive fey charm, and stolen names. They are villains, and the campaign treats their control as something the PCs can see coming, resist, and break.

Table rule — enthrallment is not consent. A character under fey enthrallment (stage 2 or higher on the track below) cannot consent to romance, and no romantic or intimate scene ever involves them. The Accord itself agrees: any kiss-oath sealed under enthrallment is a forgery the Hall of Vows will annul. Dark fey "seduction" happens on-screen only as glamour, flattery, manipulation, and menace. Romance between free, clear-headed adults, fey or mortal, remains welcome and fades to black.

scenes.title: The Courts of the Fair Folk
scenes.html:
Court Seat Ruler Stance toward Vesperine
The Dusk Court A palace "just behind the sunset," reachable through the Lanternwood at twilight The Fae Duke of the Dusk, never seen directly, only as roses and a voice Creditor. Wants the city's founding bloodlines when the Accord fails.
The Moth Court The Cocoon Palace, Lanternwood Queen Ilysse of the Hush (Part 5, Side Adventure 2) A vassal of the Dusk Court. Pressed by the Duke to harvest ever more dreams, which explains her recent gorging.
The Hedgefolk Everywhere: hedgerows, fountains, gardens, canal-weeds No one, and proud of it Free fey who flirt with the city for fun. Easily bribed with sweets, songs, and compliments.
The Thornwake A sunken ballroom under Cypress Isle, reached through the Sable Crypt Lady Nocturne Vesh The Duke's secret police of seduction. Harvests names and vows for the Night 7 collection.

How it ties to Prince Caelum. Caelum is the Duke's youngest son, and Lady Nocturne is his father's Mistress of Glamours and his bitterest rival. She has guessed that Caelum wants the city for himself, and she plans to expose him to the Duke on Night 7 while delivering Vesperine's stolen names herself. Caelum and Nocturne are each trying to use the PCs against the other. A clever party can play them off against each other.

How it ties to the murder. Thirty-one years ago it was Nocturne who whispered the trick to young Aurel Fenn: that a wedding vow of "everything I am is yours" could be read literally. Her price was Aurel's own true name, which is why Aurelian's corpse, under speak with dead, cannot say his birth name. She holds it in a jar of black glass. This is a secret for very late reveals; it changes nothing about who killed him.

scenes.title: The Fey Enthrallment Mechanic
scenes.html:
Fey control is tracked per victim and per fey on the Enthrallment Track (0–5). A character can be enthralled by several fey at once, each on its own track.

What Adds Enthrallment

Each trigger below calls for a Wisdom saving throw against the fey's DC (spell save DC, or 12 for Hedgefolk / 14 for Moth Court / 16–18 for the Thornwake). On a failure, gain 1 Enthrallment with that fey. Triggers marked † add Enthrallment automatically, with no save, because the victim chose them.

  • Accepting a fey's gift † (unless something is given in fair return)
  • Eating or drinking fey food or wine †
  • Receiving a fey's kiss (willing †) or blown kiss (save)
  • Saying your full name to a fey †
  • Thanking a fey ("thank you" implies a debt) †
  • Failing a save against a fey's charm, song, or glamour
  • Dancing with a fey until the music ends †
  • Taking glimmer (each dose) †

The Five Stages

Stage Name Effect on the victim Warning signs others can notice (Insight or Medicine DC 13, or automatic at stage 3+)
1 Smitten Daydreams of the fey; disadvantage on Perception checks to notice them approaching (you want them to surprise you). Humming the fey's tune; a faint scent of their flowers; glittering pupils.
2 Beguiled Disadvantage on Insight checks against the fey; defends them in conversation; cannot consent to romance (table rule). Speaking in half-rhymes; flinching from iron; losing small stretches of time.
3 Enthralled Charmed by the fey. Follows one suggestion from them per day. Will not willingly reveal the fey's secrets. The fey's colors appear in their clothing; their reflection wears a crown of the fey's flowers (an oathless traveler's reflection may try to warn them).
4 Bound Any vow the fey requests is "sealed" (a forged kiss-oath; see Freeing Victims). The victim acts as the fey's agent when the fey is within 1 mile; the GM may take control in key scenes. Cold hands; no shadow at noon; they no longer use their own name.
5 Nameless Their true name is stolen and kept by the fey (in a jar, a jewel, or the Book). Friends must succeed on a DC 15 Intelligence check to remember who they are. The victim becomes an NPC servant of the fey until freed. Others' memories of them blur; their handwriting vanishes from letters.

Glimmer Craving (addiction). A creature who has taken glimmer must make a DC 13 Constitution save at each dawn. On a failure, it gains 1 level of exhaustion that can't be removed while the craving lasts, and has disadvantage on saves against the Sorrowkiss and Nocturne. Three successful dawn saves in a row end the craving. Lesser restoration grants advantage on the next save, and greater restoration ends the craving outright.

Player agency. Tell players when their character gains Enthrallment, and describe the pull vividly. Players may choose to have their character struggle; at stages 1–3 a PC can spend Inspiration to ignore one fey suggestion. The danger should be dramatic, not a loss of the player's game.

Counter-Charms & Protections

Counter Effect
Cold iron Carrying it: advantage on saves against fey charm. Touching iron to an enthralled victim: an immediate new save to reduce Enthrallment by 1 (once per victim per day). Cold-iron weapons hurt Thorns badly.
A true name, spoken thrice Call an enthralled friend by their full true name three times: they get a new save with advantage, reducing Enthrallment by 1 on a success (by 2 if the caller loves them).
Cold water Dunking or splashing a victim's face ends charmed and sleep effects from fey and grants a new save. (Ondine hates this.)
Refusing gifts Politely refuse the same fey's gift three times and you're immune to that fey's gift and food triggers for 24 hours. Rudeness doesn't count; it must be gracious.
Fair exchange Pay for a fey gift with something of equal value and it adds no Enthrallment. Haggling is encouraged.
Never "thank you" Say "I'm grateful," "you're kind," or "I'll remember this" instead. Players who slip up should be teased mercilessly.
Clothes inside out Advantage on saves against glamours and illusions (and disadvantage on Charisma checks with mortals, who think you're ridiculous).
Bread and salt Under a mortal host's roof, fey who accept bread and salt cannot use charm on that household for the night.
Laughter Fey glamours can't stand mockery. A Performance (Comedy) check vs. the fey's spell DC makes the glamour flicker: everyone sees their true form for 1 round, and Thorns have disadvantage on their next charm.
The Oathless Glass and its shards Mirrors linked to the Glass show fey in their true forms. A shard held up to a victim lets them see the fey's true face (new save, advantage).
A freely given true kiss The Accord's oldest law: a kiss freely given in genuine love, with the victim's consent given before enthrallment or by a sincere standing promise between partners, outranks a fey kiss. It can end stage 1–4 Enthrallment once per campaign per victim, at the GM's discretion. Never forced, and never a kiss on someone who can't currently agree; a hand-kiss or brow-kiss is enough.

Freeing Victims

  • Distance and rest. Each long rest at least 1 mile from the fey reduces Enthrallment by 1 (only at stages 1–3).
  • Magic. Remove curse or calm emotions ends stages 1–2. Greater restoration, dispel evil and good, or break enchantment-style effects end stages 1–4.
  • Annul the forged vow. A vow sealed by a victim at stage 2+ is a forgery. Bring the victim (or proof of their enthrallment) to the Hall of Vows; the Veiled Sisters can strike it from the Ledger (the Ledger must have a keeper, or a PC must succeed on a DC 16 Religion check on Nights 1–6 while it's bleeding).
  • Recover the name (stage 5). Steal or win back the name-jar, jewel, or Book page that holds it, and speak the name to the victim. Nocturne's name-jars rest in the Thornwake's sunken ballroom under Cypress Isle, reached through the Sable Crypt (Part 3).
  • Outwit the fey. Any fey will release a victim if beaten in a fair riddle contest, wager, or bargain. Fey cannot refuse a properly formal challenge ("By the Accord of Lips, I challenge you for their name").
  • Defeat the fey. Killing or banishing the fey ends all Enthrallment it holds, but victims at stage 3+ suffer withdrawal (1 level of exhaustion and a lingering longing for 1d4 days).
  • Freely released. Caelum, Ilysse, or a turned Tempter can release victims on their own initiative, which is a powerful reward for befriending them.

Dark Fey Dungeon: The Thornwake Ballroom (Optional Lair)

Beneath the Sable Crypt, a stair of black roses descends to a sunken ballroom that the city forgot three centuries ago.

  1. The Rose Stair. Black roses with thorns (DC 13 Dex or 1d6 piercing and +1 Enthrallment from the scent). Cold iron cuts the thorns harmlessly.
  2. The Hall of Partners. Enthralled Vesperine nobles dance mindlessly in their finest clothes (use noble stat blocks; they don't fight but block the way). Calling their names thrice wakes them one at a time.
  3. The Mirror Gallery. Dozens of mirrors show each PC the person they wish they were, beckoning (DC 15 Wis or step in and be stuck for 1 hour). A Glass shard reveals the real exit.
  4. The Glimmer Vats. Silver dust refined from Moth Court dream-powder. Destroying the vats cripples the Sorrowkiss's supply. Proof here turns Queen Ilysse against the Thornwake.
  5. The Name-Jar Cellar. Hundreds of black glass jars, each humming with a whispered name, including Aurel Fenn. A riddle guards the shelves (below).
  6. The Black Throne. Nocturne's audience hall. She is here on Nights 5–7.

Riddle of the Name-Jars (whispered by every jar at once):

I'm given to you, yet others use me more;
I'm carved on your grave and called at your door.
Lose me and live, but you'll answer to none —
what can be stolen by kissing someone?

Answer: Your name. Speaking the answer makes each jar glow when its owner's friend or kin comes near, which makes it easy to find the right ones.

Resolving the Thornwake

  • Combat: Nocturne (CR 11) and the Sorrowkiss (CR 7) together are deadly. Separate them, bring cold iron, and fight in daylight if you can (in sunlight, Thorns lose resistance).
  • Charm: It cannot be done with Nocturne; she is the seducer and never the seduced. Merrow Ashgrave can be reached, though: open grief and honesty (Persuasion DC 17 with Sorrow's Mercy active) can make him lay down his sword.
  • Stealth: Slip down the Rose Stair during her Night 6 masquerade, recover the name-jars, and escape.
  • Bargain: Bring Caelum's secret to Nocturne, or Nocturne's plan to Caelum. Either fey will trade generously for leverage over the other. Or catch Nocturne in her own fine print and formally challenge her for the names.

scenes.title: Glamours & Reveals — How Glamours Work
scenes.html:
In Vesperine, the Fair Folk rarely walk the streets in their true shapes. Since the Accord began to unravel, eight of them have taken human guises: names, jobs, and faces that let them move through salons, taverns, and wakes unremarked. To the people of Carnelia, and to travelers who have just come through the Oathless Glass, they look like ordinary (if unusually charming) humans. Play them that way. Let the players like them, trust them, flirt with them, before the mask comes off.

  • The Guise. A fey's human guise is an illusion that also fools touch, smell, and sound. It is not a spell that detect magic reveals at a glance; it is part of what the fey is. True seeing, a shard of the Oathless Glass, or a successful Insight check against the fey's Glamour DC (listed below) lets one viewer see through it. That viewer then knows the truth, but everyone else still sees the human.
  • The Mirror Rule. Reflections always show the true face (Part 2). Fey in disguise avoid mirrors, still water, and polished silver: they drape mirrors, stand with their backs to windows, and ripple the wine in their glass. A PC who deliberately watches a fey's reflection needs a Perception check (DC 10 in good light, DC 15 in candlelight or a crowd) to catch a clear look. On a success, they see the true form in the glass. Oathless travelers (Glass-Marked PCs) have advantage on this check, because the Glass "wants" them to see.
  • Cold Iron. Every disguised fey reacts to cold iron: a flinch, a hiss, a burn mark, gloves that never come off. Touching cold iron to a disguised fey's bare skin forces a DC 15 Charisma saving throw. On a failure, its glamour flickers for 1 round, and everyone present glimpses the true form.
  • Tells. Each fey has small, recurring tells. Reward players who notice patterns across sessions; you might give a free Allure box or Inspiration to the first player who says "Wait. Have we ever seen her near a mirror?"
  • Reveal Shock (optional). When a fey drops its glamour dramatically, each mortal witness who didn't already know makes a DC 12 Wisdom saving throw or is frightened (Thorns) or charmed (Tempters) until the end of its next turn. The shock of beauty, or of betrayal, hits hard.
  • Relationships carry over. Allure and Enthrallment earned with the human guise apply to the true fey. A PC who flirted with "Pip the barmaid" has been flirting with Pipwhistle all along, and Enthrallment gained from the guise counts in full. Any romance that happened while a PC was unaware they were dealing with a fey is grounds for a sharp in-world grievance, and the Accord would let the PC void any kiss-oath sealed under that deception.

The eight guises, their tells and reveal triggers are in the Secrets tab; each disguised fey also has a Reveal toggle in the NPCs tab.

scenes.title: The Fey in the Endgame
scenes.html:
Night Fey escalation
1–2 Hedgefolk mischief rises. Pipwhistle and friends steal buttons and promises; Rillo plays at the revels.
3 Glimmer appears in the Drowned Market. The Sorrowkiss is seen comforting mourners in Lanternside.
4 Nocturne's masquerade invitations arrive, black envelopes sealed with a lip-print, for every noble house and the PCs.
5 Amaranth begins collecting names openly. Caelum seeks the PCs out, worried.
6 Nocturne's Masquerade in the Thornwake (or the Velvet Opera, if the Thornwake has been raided). Her attempt to enthrall a PC.
7 Amaranth reads the Book of Forfeit Names at the Opera Council vote. Nocturne denounces Caelum to the Duke's roses. Every name freed, vow annulled, or Thorn defeated before now weakens the Duke's claim.

Endgame effects:

  • If Nocturne still holds the names of three or more Council members, they vote as she commands. The Syndicate's candidate or an enthralled PC becomes Oathwarden, and the ending tilts toward Ending D.
